title: Add native support for transforming video frames without affecting `<video>` controls

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
(fyi, AI generated)

## Problem

Currently, the only common way to mirror or rotate a live camera preview in the browser is by applying a CSS transform directly to the `<video>` element:

```css
video {
    transform: scaleX(-1);
}
```

However, this transforms the entire `<video>` element, including the browser's native media controls.

This creates several usability issues:

* Play/pause buttons become mirrored.
* The timeline direction becomes visually reversed.
* Volume and fullscreen controls are flipped.
* Any future browser-provided video UI would also be transformed.

The expected behavior is that only the **rendered video frames** should be transformed, while the browser UI should remain normal.

Conceptually, the browser should treat these as separate layers:

```
+--------------------------------+
|                                |
|        Video frames            |
|   (mirror / rotate applies)    |
|                                |
+--------------------------------+
|  ▶ ───────────── 🔊 ⛶          |
|  Native video controls         |
|  (never transformed)           |
+--------------------------------+
```

---

# Use cases

## Front-facing camera previews

The most common use case is a front-facing camera.

Users expect a selfie/webcam preview to behave like a mirror:

* Moving the right hand should appear on the right side.
* Text and orientation should feel natural while positioning the camera.

However, this should normally only affect the local preview.

The actual media stream should remain unchanged.

For example, in a WebRTC video call:

```
Local preview:
    mirrored ✅

Outgoing WebRTC stream:
    unchanged ✅

Remote user's view:
    normal orientation ✅
```

The remote participant should not receive a mirrored video stream.

---

## QR scanners and document scanners

Another common use case is applications that only use the camera locally:

* QR code scanners
* Barcode scanners
* Document scanners
* OCR applications

In these cases the application often needs to adjust the presentation of the camera image without modifying the actual media stream.

---

## Hardware cameras

Many cameras are mounted in unusual orientations:

* USB webcams mounted upside down.
* Industrial inspection cameras.
* Microscopes.
* Endoscopic cameras.

Applications often need:

* Horizontal flip.
* Vertical flip.
* Rotation by 90°, 180°, 270°.

Currently developers must manually apply CSS transforms, which affects the whole video element.

---

# Possible solutions

## Option 1: CSS property

Introduce a video-specific CSS property:

```css
video {
    video-mirror: auto;
}
```

or a more generic approach:

```css
video {
    video-transform: mirror-x rotate(90deg);
}
```

Advantages:

* Keeps media capture and presentation separate.
* Fits naturally into the browser rendering model.
* Works with any source (`MediaStream`, file playback, etc.).
* Native controls remain unaffected.

Possible values:

```css
video-transform: none;

video-transform: mirror-x;

video-transform: mirror-y;

video-transform: rotate(90deg);

video-transform: mirror-x rotate(180deg);
```

---

## Option 2: HTML attribute

A declarative attribute:

```html
<video
    autoplay
    playsinline
    controls
    mirror="auto">
</video>
```

Possible values:

```html
mirror="none"

mirror="horizontal"

mirror="vertical"

mirror="auto"
```

Where:

* `auto` mirrors only front-facing cameras.
* Rear cameras remain unchanged.

---

## Option 3: Media constraints

A possible Media Capture API extension:

```javascript
navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({
    video: {
        mirrorPreview: true
    }
})
```

or:

```javascript
navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({
    video: {
        facingMode: "user",
        mirrorPreview: "auto"
    }
})
```

However, this approach has some concerns:

* Mirroring is a presentation decision, not a capture decision.
* The same MediaStream can be sent through WebRTC.
* The browser must ensure this does not modify the actual transmitted video frames.

If implemented, this should only affect local rendering.

---

# Native browser controls

Another possible improvement would be adding native video controls for orientation:

Examples:

```
Flip horizontally
Flip vertically
Rotate 90°
Rotate 180°
Rotate 270°
```

Similar to how image viewers and document scanners already work.

These operations should:

* Affect only the displayed video frames.
* Not modify the underlying MediaStream.
* Not affect WebRTC transmission.
* Not affect recordings.

---

# Important considerations

## Do not modify the actual MediaStream

A very important requirement is that this should be a rendering feature.

Example:

```text
Camera sensor
      |
      v
MediaStream
      |
      +----------------+
      |                |
      v                v
Local preview       WebRTC sender

mirrored            unchanged
```

A user should be able to mirror their own preview without accidentally sending a mirrored video to another person.

---

## Automatically detect front-facing cameras

For `mirror="auto"` or equivalent behavior:

Expected:

```javascript
facingMode: "user"
    -> mirror preview

facingMode: "environment"
    -> normal preview
```

A rear camera should never be mirrored by default.

---

# Summary

The current workaround (`transform: scaleX(-1)`) is problematic because it transforms the entire `<video>` element.

A native solution should allow browsers to transform only the rendered video frames while keeping browser UI and controls untouched.

This would simplify many existing applications and provide a consistent solution for:

* webcam previews
* video conferencing
* QR scanners
* document scanners
* camera-based applications
* specialized hardware cameras

A dedicated video rendering transform API would solve this cleanly while preserving the separation between media capture and presentation.
